reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / American Academy of Ophthalmology BCSC (External Disease and Cornea)
clinicalPearls: A chronic, bilateral, progressive cicatrising conjunctivitis, usually affecting older adults and more common in women
Early signs include chronic redness, irritation and a papillary or subtle scarring conjunctivitis that is easily mistaken for dry eye or chronic conjunctivitis
Progressive subconjunctival fibrosis causes fornix shortening (symblepharon), which is a key clinical marker of disease stage
Advanced disease leads to trichiasis, entropion, keratinisation, limbal stem cell failure, corneal scarring and blindness
Part of a systemic autoimmune blistering disorder that can also involve oral, nasopharyngeal, oesophageal and genital mucosae and the skin
Diagnosis is confirmed by conjunctival biopsy with direct immunofluorescence showing linear deposition of immunoglobulin and complement along the basement membrane zone
Management principles rely on systemic immunosuppression to halt progression, as topical therapy alone does not control the underlying inflammation
Ocular surgery can paradoxically flare disease, so inflammation should be controlled before any lid or surface procedure
reference.pathophysiology: Ocular cicatricial pemphigoid is an autoimmune type II hypersensitivity disorder in which autoantibodies are directed against components of the epithelial basement membrane zone of mucous membranes. Antibody and complement deposition triggers chronic subepithelial inflammation and activation of fibroblasts, leading to progressive subconjunctival fibrosis and scarring. This cicatrisation destroys goblet cells and accessory lacrimal tissue, shortens the fornices and produces symblepharon, while lid malposition and trichiasis further damage the ocular surface. Loss of limbal stem cells and severe aqueous and mucin deficiency culminate in corneal keratinisation, scarring and blindness.
additionalDifferentials: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis with ocular scarring
Chemical or thermal ocular surface burns
Graft-versus-host disease affecting the ocular surface
additionalInvestigations: Conjunctival biopsy with direct immunofluorescence for linear basement membrane immunoreactant deposition
Serial documentation of fornix depth and symblepharon to stage and monitor disease
Slit-lamp assessment of tear film, corneal surface and lid margins
Systemic review and referral for oral, nasopharyngeal, oesophageal and cutaneous mucosal involvement
Serological testing for circulating anti-basement membrane antibodies where available
Assessment of limbal stem cell function before considering surgical intervention
redFlags: Rapidly progressive fornix shortening or corneal involvement indicating aggressive disease
Oesophageal or laryngeal mucosal involvement risking stricture and airway compromise
Corneal ulceration or perforation from surface failure
Acute worsening after ocular surgery signalling a disease flare
reference.prognosis: Without systemic immunosuppression the disease tends to progress relentlessly to bilateral blindness, but early control of inflammation can arrest scarring and preserve vision; established cicatricial damage is generally irreversible.
pitfalls: Attributing chronic conjunctival inflammation to dry eye and missing early cicatrisation
Relying on topical therapy alone when systemic immunosuppression is required
Operating on lids or the ocular surface during active inflammation and precipitating a flare
Overlooking a drug-induced pseudopemphigoid pattern from chronic topical medication
Failing to screen for extraocular mucosal disease that carries its own morbidity
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course
